source.title: A comparative analysis of optimization and generalization properties of two-layer neural network and random feature models under gradient descent dynamics
source.authors: W. E; Chao Ma; Lei Wu

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or corruption.
record.tranche_reason: The paper's numerical experiment trains a two-layer ReLU network with gradient descent on uniformly random labels and reports its training-loss curves. Its main theoretical results also address arbitrary labels, but do not empirically measure the claim's test error or the other claim versions.
record.gate_note: The random-label training curves and the stated arbitrary-label convergence result bear on V1. No test-error-at-chance result is reported for the random-label experiment. The paper does not test training time against true labels, shuffled or Gaussian inputs, a sweep of label corruption, explicit regularizers, or the order in which true and noisy labels are learned. Cited results from Zhang et al. are not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures fitting independent random regression targets and proves convergence to zero empirical risk for arbitrary bounded targets under specified assumptions. This bears on V1's fitting component using two-layer ReLU networks and gradient descent dynamics.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate, but RKHS membership should be framed as a condition for dimension-independent generalization guarantees, rather than a necessary condition for every instance of generalization. The authors prove arbitrary-target fitting in the heavily overparameterized regime, establish closeness to an associated kernel method under suitable initialization scaling, and show worst-case dimensionality limitations over Barron-space targets. They also obtain early-stopping generalization bounds under target-function assumptions.
record.recipe_differences: The numerical experiment uses a two-layer ReLU network and gradient descent dynamics with random labels; it is a theoretical and numerical analysis, not a direct reproduction of the original image-classification experiments. The theorem studies arbitrary labels in a specified spherical-input setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The random-label experiment reports six initialization magnitudes; all are described as converging exponentially fast. The stated theory depends on the over-parameterization and initialization assumptions.

fits_no_version.finding: For a noiseless one-neuron regression target, wide unregularized networks generalize worse than a model using a crafted path-norm penalty; narrow unregularized networks generalize well.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalization under gradient descent can depend on network width, initialization, target alignment, and a specifically chosen explicit penalty.

record.problems: The random-label numerical experiment uses n=50, d=50 and one width, and reports curves rather than exact loss values. It does not report test error or compare random-label training time with true-label training. The theorem is conditional on its assumptions and supplies no random-label test-error result.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying results identified. Figure 1's individual curve values were not separately extracted because they are figure-only; R1 records the authors' textual aggregate description.

untested.parts: Chance-level classification test error, standard deep classification architectures, stochastic-gradient training, and unchanged hyperparameters relative to a matched true-label experiment.
The training-time ratio between random and true labels and slowing across increasing corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily worsening test error across a label-corruption sweep.
The effects of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation on random-label fitting and of removing those interventions on true-label generalization.
The order in which networks learn shared real patterns and memorize noisy labels.

record.verdict_notes: Fast absolute convergence does not establish V2's comparison with true-label training. The path-norm regularization comparison does not directly test V5's named interventions. Untested classification and optimizer details do not turn the positive random-target fitting results into scope-limiting verdicts.

versions.untested_parts: The random-label experiment does not report test error or compare directly with true-label training. The theorem's arbitrary-label statement is not a test-error measurement.
No comparison of training time for true versus random labels or convergence rate across corruption fractions.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel or Gaussian-noise input experiment.
No sweep over fractions of corrupted labels or paired training and test errors.
No experiment testing weight decay, dropout or data augmentation against random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
No measurement of the order or relative timing of learning real patterns and memorizing noise.

rows.subject: two-layer neural network models
rows.operation_detail: Gradient descent dynamics on uniformly sampled inputs with labels uniformly drawn from [-1, 1]; six initialization magnitudes are plotted.

conditions.value: β=0, β=1/m, β=1/m², β=1, β=m², β=m

rows.value: Figure 1 shows training loss converging exponentially fast for all initializations considered.
rows.note: The text describes the curves as consistent with Theorem 3.2; exact per-initialization loss values are figure-only.
rows.check: The targets are continuous uniform draws from [-1,1], and the measure is squared training loss, not classification error. The flattened Figure 1 legend appears to have misrendered fractional exponents: the six initialization scales are 0, 1/m, 1/sqrt(m), 1, sqrt(m), and m, rather than including 1/m² and m². Exact terminal losses cannot be recovered from the supplied figure text; the authors explicitly report exponential convergence for all six.

rows.subject: two-layer neural network models
rows.size_stated: over-parametrized; width requirement m ≳ λ_n⁻⁴ n² δ⁻¹ ln(n²/δ)
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 3.2 bounds empirical risk under gradient descent for arbitrary labels.

conditions.value: random initialization as specified in the setup

rows.value: R̂_n(Θ_t) ≤ exp(−m(λ_n^(a)+β²λ_n^(b))t) R̂_n(Θ₀), for any t ≥ 0
rows.uncertainty: Probability at least 1−δ over random initialization
rows.note: The theorem establishes convergence to zero empirical risk for arbitrary labels in its stated over-parameterized setting; it does not give test error.
rows.check: This is a theoretical guarantee for continuous-time gradient flow, not an empirical stochastic-gradient result. State its input assumptions explicitly: unit-norm inputs, bounded targets, and positive minimum eigenvalues of both specified kernel matrices, together with the width and initialization requirements. Arbitrary labels does not mean arbitrary datasets without these assumptions.

relationships.condition: Random continuous targets; two-layer ReLU network with n=50, d=50, m=10,000; six initialization scales.
relationships.reason: R1 reports exponentially converging training loss for every initialization considered, supporting random-target fitting in this regression setting.
relationships.display_finding: Training loss converged exponentially for every initialization scale tested.

relationships.condition: Arbitrary bounded targets under Theorem 3.2's kernel nondegeneracy, width, and initialization assumptions.
relationships.reason: R2 guarantees exponential decay of squared empirical risk to zero with probability at least 1−δ over initialization.
relationships.display_finding: Under the theorem's kernel, width, and initialization assumptions, squared empirical risk decays exponentially to zero with probability at least 1−δ over initialization.
